name: Dana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana Gupta, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines for years since my vocational certificate and apprenticeship. I know the narrow South Steps route and how to test a service line, and I like handing a lit street back to people; I still keep a printed circuit sheet in the truck.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A wet tablet once went dark while we were at South Steps. The paper number and dispatch confirmation helped us verify the switch before anyone worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a shorter work order is welcome, but the line still needs someone to measure and repair it. I would keep the old circuit sheet in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, the quiet future sounds manageable. I've done line repairs since my apprenticeship, my pay is ordinary but reliable, and Mira and I have about four months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my usual field rota and the same household savings transfer each pay day. In the first year I'd check that the printed circuit sheets stay in the trucks; I won't learn an AI tool merely to rewrite a report I can already make clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the job and aware that a storm can still upset any plan. Our children are grown, and Mira's hospital porter work brings another steady wage for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the paper sheet help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the South Steps pole, a wet tablet went dark while we checked the service line. The paper circuit number let us confirm the right switch with dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI outside the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I've never used AI tools. If the company changes a safety process, I want training and a worker check before anyone asks me to trust it.

say: I'd welcome **shorter work orders** after safe repairs for the crew on call.
I'd keep **printed circuit sheets** available for field crews.
think: My **ordinary wage** and four months of savings make a small change manageable.
Mira's **porter work** adds a second dependable wage for now.
do: Continue the **usual field rota** and maintain normal savings transfers.
Check that **printed circuit sheets** remain in crew trucks through the first year.
feel: **Settled**, with ordinary storm uncertainty still in mind.
S0.quote: The paper circuit number let us confirm the right switch with dispatch.
fieldNote: Dana's **paper backup** proved useful during a wet tablet failure at South Steps, explaining her practical resistance to new tools.
Four months of **savings** and two current wages support calm while she remains aware of storm-related work uncertainty.

steps.text: Continue the usual line repair rota and normal household savings transfers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management that dispatchers must test any new scheduling screen before jobs are changed. Our repair crews need their knowledge of the narrow streets as much as a quick route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking tasks in the office may move fast, while Mira's porter work and my field repairs look safe for now. I still wonder whether fewer dispatchers would mean poorer information or fewer spare callouts for our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the next union meeting I'd ask for a joint dispatch-and-field test on the South Steps route and a written record of mistakes. In the first year I'd keep taking my usual paid repairs and ask a supervisor to confirm any new switching plan before work starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the office staff, but I don't expect a big cut to our income yet. I'd rather see real mistakes caught than argue about a screen I haven't used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is tricky about South Steps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The narrow alley is blocked by bins most mornings, and a truck needs the upper entrance. Dispatch remembers the blocked alley. A street address does not tell a truck where the bins block the alley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take part in the test without using the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I can compare its printed directions with what we find on site. A dispatcher can operate the screen and the crew can check the route.

say: I'd demand **dispatcher testing** on real local calls before scheduling jobs change.
I'd defend **local access knowledge** for narrow streets.
think: My **field pay** and Mira's porter wage look safe for now.
I worry a thinner **dispatch team** could miss hazards or reduce spare callouts.
do: Bring a **South Steps trial** proposal to the union meeting.
Keep **paid repairs** and get supervisor confirmation of new switching plans.
feel: **Uneasy** for office staff, with household wages still expected to continue.
S1.quote: A street address does not tell a truck where the bins block the alley.
fieldNote: Dana's **union proposal** gives workers a concrete way to test routes without requiring her to use AI herself.
Her **household wages appear safe** in this slower robot picture, but office cuts could harm field information.

steps.text: Propose a South Steps dispatch-and-crew trial at the union meeting
Continue paid repairs and confirm switching plans with the supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 may handle orders and plans, but field robots around 2031 could take our repair work. The company should bargain over safety checks and paid alternative work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots can mend lines, and I may still need wages. Mira's hospital porter job could face the same machines. Four months saved gives us time to search, not enough to retire on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union to seek a written field staffing plan and funded inspection training. In 2029 I'd enroll if the utility pays for the course and keeps my wages; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for posted inspection work here and at the two other utilities within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, mostly because both of us earn with our hands. I can make applications and use the savings carefully, but I cannot assume a new inspection post is reserved for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mira tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Mira we should check the monthly bills before promising an early retirement. Our grown children can visit, but they have their own homes to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the inspection job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a paid course proved a particular tool safe, I would learn what the job requires. I have never used AI, so I would need proper training and a human safety check.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd ask for **negotiated safety checks** and paid alternative work.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when repair robots arrive.
Mira's **porter income** could also face robots, making four months saved insufficient for retirement.
do: Ask the **union** for a written staffing plan and funded inspection training.
Enroll in **paid training** if offered in 2029, then apply for posted utility inspection jobs in 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about two hands-on wages, with room to search carefully.
S2.quote: Four months saved gives us time to search, not enough to retire on.
fieldNote: Dana locates **field income risk**, three years after thinking AI, and considers Mira's porter work exposed too.
Her **training condition** requires funded tuition, continued wages and safety checks because she has never used AI tools.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate written staffing plans and paid training
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if tuition and wages are covered
Apply for posted inspection jobs at reachable utilities in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company five years should allow real robot trials and a fair agreement on what happens to crews. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66, retirement might be possible if our actual income figures cover the house. Mira's porter work could also change in 2034, so we need to know what happens if both wages stop together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request written retirement statements for us both and ask the union to include South Steps access in any robot trial. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection course if it has a recognised certificate; in 2034 I'd retire only if the figures cover housing and medicine, otherwise apply for posted inspection shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than rushed. The extra years let us test a machine and a household budget before we choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the trial to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should identify the upper entrance when the alley is blocked and stop if access is unsafe. I want the crew's notes beside the vendor's report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut back now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from ordinary groceries. I could put thirty from each regular pay packet into a separate reserve after our roof maintenance is paid, if the budget allows.

say: I'd ask for **real robot trials** and fair crew terms before 2034.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later physical repairs.
think: Retirement at **66** depends on both written income figures.
Mira's **porter job** may also change when robots can do hands-on work.
do: Request **retirement statements** and seek South Steps access testing this year.
Take a **paid inspection course** if offered in 2032, then choose retirement or posted work in 2034.
feel: **Watchful**, with years to test work and household figures.
S3.quote: I want the crew's notes beside the vendor's report.
fieldNote: Dana's **2034 choice** depends on household figures for both partners, not an assumed retirement at 66.
Her **trial demand** includes worker observations about blocked access and a stop condition when the route is unsafe.

steps.text: Compare both written retirement statements with housing and medicine costs
Ask the union to include South Steps access in robot trials
Take a paid recognised inspection course in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted inspection shifts if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger workers ten years is time to write down the awkward access points that a plan misses. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to be retired from climbing before 71 if the written numbers for Mira and me cover our bills. I still want the company to show how younger crews will work with robots. A glossy manual cannot tell a truck where the alley bins stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid line shifts and ask for updated retirement statements every year. In 2037 Mira and I would set a date if housing and medical costs fit; by 2039 I'd give the apprentices my South Steps route notes and attend a union safety meeting if the robot trial raises access problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income in the next few years and concerned for younger coworkers. A decade leaves me enough time to plan and to pass on what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the route notes say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The upper entrance takes the truck, and the alley bins block the lower approach most mornings. I'd draw the turn with measurements, not just write 'use the back'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement costs don't fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid field work if it remains and apply for an inspection vacancy before 2039. I wouldn't ask our grown children to cover the gap.

say: I'd ask workers to record **awkward access** for future crews.
I'd mark **2039 field robots** as the hands-on change when I'll be 71.
think: I may retire before **71** if both written income figures cover bills.
Younger crews still need **real safety guidance** as robots arrive.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and update retirement statements each year.
Choose a **2037 retirement date** if costs fit; pass South Steps notes to apprentices by 2039.
feel: **Calm** about near-term income, concerned for younger workers.
S4.quote: A glossy manual cannot tell a truck where the alley bins stand.
fieldNote: Dana sees **retirement before 2039** as plausible with verified household income, not as a guarantee from age alone.
Her **South Steps notes** preserve measured access details and support union safety review for younger crews.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts while updating retirement statements annually
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if housing and medical costs fit
Attend a union robot safety meeting if South Steps access problems arise

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because field robots in 2031 could reach both my repairs and Mira's porter job while we still need wages. Paid inspection training, written staffing plans, real utility vacancies and crew-reviewed safety trials would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stops a robot when the alley is blocked and the route has changed. The crew should still have a word before a machine touches a line.

headlineQuote: The crew should still have a word before a machine touches a line.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship who knows narrow access routes and field isolation checks.
Her **four-month reserve** support current security, alongside Mira's hospital porter income and grown children outside the home.
She **never uses AI tools** and wants union-reviewed route tests, printed circuit backups and worker notes in robot trials.
The **2031 robot date** worries her because both hands-on jobs could face cuts before retirement is affordable.
Longer warning allows **written retirement checks** and a measured South Steps handover to newer crews.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Dana most because 2031 robots could threaten both her repair wage and Mira's porter income.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid inspection training**, written staffing plans, posted utility jobs and crew-reviewed safety trials.
